title: Optimization methods for supervised machine learning: From linear models to deep learning
contribution: INFORMS tutorial that derives supervised-learning optimization problems for OR readers and surveys first-order, variance-reduced, quasi-Newton, Hessian-free and subsampled/random-model methods, ending with Scheinberg's random-model framework as the route for adaptive second-order methods in ML.
problem_entry: Community gap: barriers of terminology, goals and collaboration between statistics, CS and optimization; the tractable problem is derived as a chain from maximizing the probability of a correct prediction to regularized empirical risk (pp. 1, 3-7).
key_idea: For each classical deterministic method, name the ML cost that breaks it (full-data passes, dense Hessians, nonconvexity) and present the stochastic repair; random-model results keep deterministic rates if estimates are accurate enough with some positive probability, with sample size tied to step length or radius (pp. 8-22).
assumptions: Convex loss and regularizer in Sec. 2, strong convexity/L-smoothness for quoted rates, 'sample indefinitely' for the SGD trade-off argument (flagged as only a theoretical guideline for fixed data sets); two-moment condition (mu1, mu2) for stochastic quasi-Newton (pp. 7-11, 15-16).
proof_devices: Bousquet-Bottou error-budget split: estimation error <= eps/2 and optimization error <= eps/2 so n >= O(1/eps^2) (eqs. 17-18, p. 10)
complexity tables with a common iteration measure in n, kappa, eps (Tables 2-3, p. 13)
generic two-inequality sufficient condition for a preconditioned stochastic step to keep SGD rates (p. 15)
experiments: none (points to a Lehigh thesis comparison of Hessian-free trust-region solvers, p. 21)
positioning: Builds on Bottou-Curtis-Nocedal and Bousquet-Bottou; fair to SGD in theory, critical in practice; groups her random-model papers with Gratton-Royer-Vicente-Zhang as one framework; STORM ref lists first author as 'C. Chen' (pp. 10-11, 21-23).
writing: Tutorial voice: glossary table and business toy example before formulas, boxed pseudocode, explicit hedges ('to the best of our knowledge', 'In truth, we cannot be sure.'), no theorems (pp. 2, 11, 19).
limits_future: No conclusion section (ends in Sec. 3.4, p. 22); open questions: stochastic momentum guarantees, provably better practical second-order methods, avoiding saddles/poor minima in DNNs, learning bounds useless when C >> n, negative-curvature experiments (pp. 11, 15, 20, 21).

method_links.note: Stated (2017): random-model results require |S_k| large relative to the step length / trust-region radius; accuracy hierarchy Hessian < gradient < function value.

Stated: line search well known to perform well; SGD very sensitive to parameter choices; for nonconvex problems evaluating F is essential (trust-region accept/reject). Earlier than the 2020 IEEE SPM statement cited in SKILL.md.
Stated deterministic parity: random-model methods 'retain their convergence rates'; subsampled Newton rates 'similar to their deterministic counterparts'.
Explicit community bridging, but ML <-> OR for first/second-order methods rather than DFO <-> zeroth-order.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sampled Hessians need much looser sample sizes than sampled gradients; F estimates need even stronger ones (also S012 p. 9: estimates tighter than models).

Summarize competitors in a complexity table with one common measure (Tables 2-3, p. 13).
Check a new preconditioned stochastic step against the generic (mu1, mu2) two-inequality condition and watch for correlation between B_k and the gradient sample (pp. 15-16).

title: SGD and Hogwild! convergence without the bounded gradients assumption
contribution: Shows the bounded-stochastic-gradient assumption contradicts strong convexity, replaces it with a bound derived from per-sample L-smoothness (and convexity), proves a.s. convergence and O(1/t) rates for SGD with a larger admissible step, and gives the first diminishing-step O(1/t) analysis of Hogwild! with inconsistent reads via a general filtered recursion.
problem_entry: A standard assumption (E||grad f(w;xi)||^2 <= sigma^2) is shown in three lines to contradict strong convexity, plus a 1-D counterexample along SGD iterates; Bottou et al.'s (M, N) alternative has unknown constants that set the step (p. 2).
key_idea: In expected-risk minimization each realization is L-smooth (and convex), so E||grad f(w;xi)||^2 <= 4L[F(w)-F*] + 2E||grad f(w*;xi)||^2 with computable constants; SGD/Hogwild! unchanged except diminishing steps (pp. 2, 4-6).
assumptions: F mu-strongly convex; each f(.;xi) L-smooth; each f(.;xi) convex (droppable at cost kappa); xi i.i.d.; Hogwild!: consistency with delay tau, atomic entry reads/writes (pp. 2-4, 6).
proof_devices: ||a||^2 <= 2||a-b||^2 + 2||b||^2 with b = grad f(w*;xi) plus generalized Johnson-Zhang co-coercivity bound (Lemmas 1, 3, pp. 4, 10)
Robbins-Siegmund supermartingale convergence + contradiction with sum eta_t = infinity (Thm 1, pp. 11-12)
induction E||w_t-w*||^2 <= NG/(mu^2 (t+E)) with G = max{I, J}, then restart from w_T (Thm 2, pp. 12-13)
random diagonal filter matrices with d_xi E[S|xi] = D_xi unifying Hogwild! and coordinate updates (pp. 5, 13-14)
0/1 masks Sigma_{t,j} for inconsistent reads and collision probability Delta for cross terms (pp. 14-16)
unrolled linear recursion Y_{t+1} <= beta_t Y_t + gamma_t and telescoping product prod(1-2/(j+E)) (pp. 18-19)
bootstrap induction on a decreasing envelope Z_t (pp. 20-21)
experiments: L2-logistic regression (lambda = 1/n) on ijcnn1 and covtype; single-core simulation of Hogwild! recursion, 10 runs averaged, filter fraction sweep with tau = 10 and tau in {1, 10, 100}; x-axes coordinate updates and epochs; no baselines (pp. 7-8).
positioning: Bounded-gradient literature called 'clearly false' under strong convexity; corrects Bottou et al. 2016 constants (step larger by L/mu); credits Moulines-Bach; Mania et al.'s removal 'only mentioned as a remark without proof'; Leblond et al. 2018 as closest, differences listed (pp. 2-5).
writing: Nested contribution bullets; 'Here we make an important observation'; remarks compare constants and explain surprises with a thought experiment; one loose intro claim of probability-one convergence for the diminishing-step analysis while Hogwild! result is only in expectation (pp. 2-7).
limits_future: Conclusion is summary only with no future directions (p. 8); visible limits: strong convexity of F required, step needs mu, bounded delay, no multi-core timing (pp. 2, 4, 6, 7).

method_links.note: Oracle property (second-moment bound) derived from per-sample structure instead of assumed, but in expectation rather than a probability-p accuracy contract.
Exploits structure of ML expected risk (each realization smooth/convex) to replace a generic noise assumption.
Practitioner method (SGD, Hogwild!) kept unchanged, only the analysis changes; but non-adaptive with pre-specified diminishing steps.
Step schedule is pre-specified but computed from known mu and L, not hand-tuned; sold as the advantage over unknown M or sigma.
Supermartingale (Robbins-Siegmund) for a.s. convergence and induction for O(1/t); no adaptive step parameter or stopping-time argument.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Three-line proof that bounded stochastic gradients contradict strong convexity plus a 1-D counterexample along SGD iterates, then replacement by a derived bound; similar minimal-counterexample moves in S031 (separable data, p. 8) and S004 (six points on a circle, pp. 7-8).

transferable: Before relaxing a standard assumption, prove it contradicts your setting (three lines) and add a 1-D counterexample along the algorithm's actual iterates (p. 2).

Prove O(1/(t+E)) by induction with G = max{initial-gap term, alpha^2/(alpha-1)}, then restart from w_T to separate transient and asymptotic regimes (pp. 12-13).
Unify algorithm variants as one recursion with a random filter satisfying an unbiasedness identity; read variants off as parameter extremes and keep leading constants explicit to rank them (pp. 5-6).
Validate an asynchrony theorem by a single-core simulation injecting delay tau explicitly, plotting against both coordinate updates and epochs (pp. 7-8).
Pair a counter-intuitive theorem feature (independent of delay tau) with a thought experiment explaining it (p. 7).

title: Stochastic optimization using a trust-region method and random models
contribution: STORM: a standard trust-region method whose models and function estimates are only required to be accurate (errors proportional to delta_k and delta_k^2) with fixed probabilities alpha, beta conditioned on the past, arbitrary otherwise; proves almost-sure convergence to first-order stationarity via martingale arguments, shows how to build such models under unbiased noise and biased computation-failure noise, and tests it on CUTEr and logistic regression.
problem_entry: Gap between deterministic DFO and derivative-based stochastic optimization; SG methods need tuned parameters, SA methods need tuned sampling, fail under biased noise and outliers; motivated by randomized numerical processes that can fail (pp. 1-4, 25-26).
key_idea: Keep the trust-region algorithm; replace f by fresh random estimates f0_k, fs_k in the ratio test, add ||g_k|| >= eta2 delta_k, and require only alpha-probabilistically fully linear models and beta-probabilistically eps_F delta_k^2-accurate estimates (pp. 2, 7-9).
assumptions: Fixed (not increasing) probabilities conditioned on past sigma-algebras; arbitrary failures; f bounded below and f, grad f L-Lipschitz on an algorithm-dependent enlarged region (admitted in Remark 4.2); bounded model Hessians; eta2 step restriction used in proof but not in practice; no hidden constraints (pp. 3, 8-10, 21, 27).
proof_devices: potential Phi_k = nu f(X_k) + (1-nu) Delta_k^2 with E[Phi_{k+1}-Phi_k | F] <= -sigma Delta_k^2 giving sum Delta_k^2 < infinity a.s. (Thm 4.11, pp. 14-19)
2 x 4 case split on ||grad f|| >= zeta delta_k and outcomes of (I_k, J_k); nu chosen so all but 'both bad' are no worse than an unsuccessful step (pp. 15-19)
worst case bounded by Taylor + Lipschitz (C3 = 1 + 3L/(2 zeta)) and made rare via (1-alpha)(1-beta) small (pp. 16, 19-20)
log-radius submartingale R_k = log_gamma(delta_k/b) bounded below by +-1 walk W_k = sum(2 1_I 1_J - 1), alphabeta >= 1/2 (Thm 4.16, pp. 21-22)
submartingale dichotomy with bounded increments (Thm 4.4, Durrett, p. 10)
sum over ||grad f|| > eps of Delta_k < infinity for lim-type result (Lemma 4.17, p. 23)
Chebyshev sample size p >= V/(kappa'^2 (1-alpha') delta^4) and alpha = (alpha')^{n+1} by independence over n+1 points (p. 24)
plugging textbook constants into probability conditions: (1-alpha)(1-beta) <= 1/440 (Remark 4.13, pp. 20-21)
experiments: 53 CUTEr sum-of-squares problems with multiplicative/additive uniform noise vs own TR-SAA and TR-SAA-resample, performance profiles on function evaluations (tau = 1e-3, budget 1000(n+1), 10 runs); garbage-value computation-failure noise (30 runs, budget 10000(n+1)); theory-threshold sweep on a quadratic (n = 2, 10); logistic regression vs Adagrad on 4 datasets with one data pass (pp. 27-35).
positioning: Compares Deng-Ferris, SPSA, SCSR by assumptions (probabilities -> 1, tuned decaying parameters, unique minimizer); acknowledges Billups-Larson as 'a very similar method', lists differences, concedes their advantage, skips empirical comparison; credits Larson-Billups for estimate definition and Phi (pp. 4-6, 9, 14).
writing: Novelty sentence framed as weaker assumptions with bullets on what is not assumed; plain-language proof outline before Thm 4.11; remarks flag proof artefacts; early admission that probability bounds are 'far from tight', later tested; no conclusion section (pp. 3, 15, 18-21, 35).
limits_future: No rates ('a subject for future research'); probabilities hard to know and far from tight; eta2 forces small steps, decoupling left as more complex analysis; Lipschitz assumption on algorithm-dependent region; hidden constraints out of scope (pp. 3, 10, 18-21, 25, 27).

method_links.note: Two events I_k, J_k with accuracy proportional to delta_k and delta_k^2, fixed conditional probabilities, arbitrary failures; also evidence for the limitation that p is hard to know.

Correction: a.s. convergence needs alpha, beta close to 1 (Cor. 4.12; (1-alpha)(1-beta) <= 1/440 for textbook constants), alphabeta >= 1/2 only for the liminf step; experiments succeed with alpha ~ 0.27.
Standard trust region with standard parameters; single proof-driven repair ||g_k|| >= eta2 delta_k (not used in practice, so a proof device rather than an algorithmic change).
Stochastic-process analysis: Phi_k expected decrease and log-radius submartingale.
Only almost-sure convergence; complexity/rates explicitly deferred.
Fully linear models from well-poised sets; Algorithm 4 changes the interpolation set minimally but recomputes values afresh so garbage values do not persist.
Function-evaluation budgets and performance profiles on 53 CUTEr sum-of-squares problems (verifies a test set used by the group).
Function values under the same radius-tied contract.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Compute the theorem's minimal success probability on a toy quadratic and plot empirical success across it with the threshold marked; theory needs (1-sigma) > 0.9990 for n = 10, yet 100% success at 0.998 with alpha ~ 0.27.
Function-value estimates need tighter accuracy (eps_F <= kappa_ef and a further bound) than models; also stated in S031 p. 22.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Garbage value V = -10000 with probability sigma when |f_i| < eps; averaging optimizes the wrong function, so no averaging is done.

transferable: Write the oracle contract as two events (model good, estimates good) with fixed conditional probabilities and no assumption on failures; condition the estimate event on the sigma-algebra that already includes the current model (pp. 8-9).
Draw fresh estimates of f at both current and trial points every iteration, independent of the model data, so a lucky low value cannot lock in (pp. 7, 28).
Potential Phi_k = nu f(X_k) + (1-nu) Delta_k^2 with a 2 x 4 case split; choose nu so all but the worst case do no worse than an unsuccessful step, then make the worst case rare (pp. 14-19).
For liminf, show log_gamma(delta_k/b) is a submartingale bounded below by a +-1 walk counting good iterations (pp. 21-22).
Plug textbook parameter values into the probability conditions to show readers the size of the constants (Remark 4.13, pp. 20-21).
Theory-threshold sweep: plot empirical success vs probability of success with the theoretical threshold drawn as a line (pp. 30-32).
When a baseline violates your assumptions, build a variant removing one violation (TR-SAA-resample) to isolate the effect (p. 28).
If a concurrent paper has a near-identical method, say so, list assumption differences, concede its advantage and explain why you do not compare (pp. 5-6).
